utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are to continue with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Janicevic.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, where the headquarters of the 162nd Brigade was located, and we'd just moved on to that area of discussion towards the end of the working day on Friday.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the autumn of 1998 the headquarters did not have a set location. It moved around. They changed the location very often. And from 1998 onwards, the headquarters was stationed in Ivaja, as of November 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The village of Ivaja?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the village of Ivaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Part of the diary of Hajrusha Kurtaj, is it contained in tab 79, something that is in fact linked up to their work and existence and things of that kind? Do you have the tab before you?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just take a moment to find it, please. Did you say 79?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the diary of Hajrusha Kurtaj, the deputy commander of the Kacanik group, of that terrorist organisation while it hadn't been proclaimed the 162nd Brigade. It was seized in August when there was an attempt to arrest him and another group of terrorists in his house in the village of Gabrica, and on that occasion during the clash another two persons were killed -- two persons were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what do these documents contain? Let's go through them very quickly, Mr. Janicevic. Apart from this list of weapons, what photographs do we have here along -- attached to this diary?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are photographs of the terrorists who were trained with the 12.7 millimetre machine-gun, and it was taken in the area of Kacanik - light machine-gun, in fact - in the spring of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of insignia were there on the uniforms of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The uniforms were black and the emblems were the emblems of the KLA, UCK. One of them is wearing a uniform, an olive green uniform with a helmet. And that can be placed on the overhead projector. You'll be able to see them with a 12.7 millimetre light machine-gun and the bullet belt, bandolier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are all black and white photographs, and we're not going to waste time putting them on the overhead projector. We all have them here in the room.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the photographs and some other things here testifying to the personal relations between individual terrorists in the Kacanik group itself, we also have a list of weapons, who brought how many weapons. This probably relates to the weapons they brought in from Albania. On the 13th of July, six automatic rifles, for example, 60 to 70 rounds of ammunition. Probably they were cases of ammunition, 60 to 70 cases of ammunition. Fifty caps, 50 vests, automatic rifles, 26 combat sets -- kits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. So you have the photographs, you have described Kacanik. How would you characterise the security situation and the activities of the terrorists in that area?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kacanik, in -- or, rather, from November was an area where terrorist activity was expanding, and it intensified, terrorist attacks intensified in the area after mid-February 1999 when the first kidnappings started to occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Janicevic, tell us, how did you come by your information about the terrorist group that called itself the 162nd Brigade, about its headquarters, staff, the commander, and everything else?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the information confirming our operative information and intelligence that we had earlier on, and they were amassed on the basis of friendly contacts and sources and talking to individuals who in one way or another came into contact with members of the service, and this is a diary which confirmed everything we had learnt and knew up until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the tabs, and I'm just going to remind you of those tabs, they were 18.1, 2, 3, 17, 20, 21, 22, 23, and 27 inclusive, so within the frameworks of those tabs under tab 8 -- or, rather, 18, and the individual attachments I mentioned, do they contain information indicating the actions of the 162nd Brigade as well?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they contain information from Official Notes which indicate the organisation and work of the 162nd KLA Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to your operative knowledge, what were the tasks of that brigade and its headquarters and staff and the entire composition of the brigade as a whole?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tasks of the 162nd Brigade were organised into three stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, three stages, but tell us briefly what the first stage was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down and make pauses between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Janicevic, the interpreters are asking you to slow down and to observe the pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I think Mr. Janicevic should answer again. But before that, I didn't follow your evidence in relation to the provenance of these documents. Did you say that these photographs were seized together with this diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photographs were taken along with the diary and a lot more documents which were -- which were seized and which related to the work of the terrorist group in our state. May I be allowed to answer the question that was asked me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were three stages. The first stage was the collection of material and technical equipment to allow the organisation to function. The second stage were plans to secure the border crossings towards Macedonia, and securing the border crossing without any incidents for terrorists coming from outside and for mercenaries coming in from abroad. And the third stage was the -- were the terrorist attacks themselves, in fact, and terrorist provocations; kidnapping, abduction of citizens, the killing of Serb citizens and Albanians who did not agree with the policy being waged by the KLA. So that, then, started, to all intents and purposes, in the second half of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 18 as a whole, do we have there numerous information bearing that out?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to what was going on in that part of your area relating to Kacanik, that particular locality, the Kacanik locality, did you analyse data and information about Serbs, Albanians, and other ethnic groups killed; soldiers, policemen, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We analysed the killings per communes, local communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Looking at the municipalities, casualties with -- which ended in death and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we're not going to go back to that but that area of Kacanik was characterised how?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was characterised by the fact that along the state border, 47 kilometres of that state border, the configuration of the terrain is better than the one -- than the borderline towards Albania. It is an area where people live, as opposed to the other border belt, which is not populated and a difficult terrain, and you need much less time to cross the border illegally if you compare it to the Yugoslav-Albanian border where the terrain is difficult. So these terrorists -- the terrorists bore that in mind when they stationed their 162nd Brigade in that particular area and when they gave it the assignment of not undertaking any terrorist activities but to lie low until almost mid-February 1999, to keep a low profile in order to cover up their activities and their presence and to be able, in a semi-legal fashion or illegal fashion, to bring in weapons and volunteers and mercenaries and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, you said in explaining the tabs, tabs 51 to 59 inclusive, you said, among other things, that the same conduct was applied to who -- no matter who the casualties were; Albanians, Serbs, other ethnic groups, soldiers, policemen or whatever. Can you give us an example where the casualties were Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can give you many examples. For example, in the Stimlje municipality and that general area, Nazmija Ljui [phoen] was killed in the area of Zborce, which is two to two and a half kilometres away from Stimlje in the forest, just for the mere fact that his brother, his brother was a reservist of the police station in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 80, do we see photographs from the on-site investigation pertaining to the killing of the Albanian?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the photographs of the late Nazmija Ljui.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what are the other photographs?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other photographs are photographs from the on-site investigation conducted when his brother reported the killing. They are parts of the clothing, parts of the footwear, the cart, horse-drawn cart he was brought in, the boot, and he went to get some firewood for his family with this cart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was doing his -- going about his regular daily business. He was going to the woods to get some firewood for his family and was killed because his brother was a reservist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was an on-site investigation also conducted with respect to the killing of a number of Albanians that we mentioned earlier on whose names are found in tab 54?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is also linked to Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They're Mahmut Daliste and Camil Reka --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Mahmut Daliste is concerned, no on-site investigation was conducted because we didn't know that he'd in fact been killed. The first information reached us that he had been kidnapped, that there had been a kidnapping. It was only later that we learnt that they were killed in a brutal manner and held previously for two days in a house in a street in Kacanik or, rather, in front of a house in Kacanik and that they would instil fear into the population and show the population. They left them there to see what fate would befall them if they ally themselves with the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janicevic. Now, under point 1, deportation, paragraph 63 of the indictment, under (j) in the Serbian version, it says: "In the period from the 24th of March to the 14th of April, forces of the FRY and Serbia shelled and attacked villages in the Urosevac municipality ..." And Urosevac is the central municipality bureau and secretariat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I go on: "... including the Biba, Prelez, Raka, and Staro Selo villages, killing a number of residents. After the shelling, forces of the FRY and Serbia entered some of the villages, including Papaz and Sojevo, and ordered the residents to leave. Other Kosovo Albanians from Varos Selo and Mirosavlje fled their villages as the Serb forces entered." And then it goes on to say that: "After the residents left their homes, the soldiers and policemen burned the houses. The displaced persons went to the town of Urosevac where most boarded trains which carried them to the Macedonian border crossing at Djeneral Jankovic." And then: "Serb forces directed the train passengers to walk ... to the border. Others travelled in convoys ... At the border, Serb forces confiscated all their documents."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: The allegations here contained in this point of the indictment, and there are several allegations there, I assume you were able to follow, are any of them correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they could be correct when from the 24th of March, in all of these villages there were units of the army of Yugoslavia. How could they shell themselves? That is my first point. Secondly, Staro Selo or, rather, Sojevo in Kamena Glava, and partly Staro Selo, had tank units stationed in them. NATO Air Force bombed them every day. Three APCs were hit by NATO bombs and destroyed. Until the end of the war, the forces the army of Yugoslavia were in those villages, so I do not see how or why they could have shelled themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You've given an answer as far as the shelling is concerned. Now, since this paragraph has to do with deportations, it says that the forces of the FRY and Serbia, as they're called here, expelled residents from villages and boarded them on trains, making them go to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. As soon as the bombing started, the population started moving out of the entire area of Urosevac, especially Kacanik, where they assumed that perhaps NATO ground forces would enter the territory of Serbia. I assert that the forces of the FRY and Serbia, as they're called there, did not expel the population. There are many examples that villages in that area remained intact, that not a single inhabitant left. Rahovica, Crnoljevo, for instance, Srpski Babus. Srpski Babus is 100 per cent an ethnically pure Serb village. Not even ten residents remained. After the war, the village was razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the entire population of that Serb populated village left?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not more than ten villagers stayed. There are about 50 houses there and no one was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those were Serb houses?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were Serb houses. About 150 Albanian houses and 50 Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as for paragraph 63, what I quoted, you can testify to the fact that none of this is correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely none of it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On several occasions in the territory of your SUP, as we saw a few moments ago, you had the opportunity of seizing documentation of terrorist groups and their staffs, no matter what they called themselves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. After every anti-terrorist action, for the most part, in their staffs and substaffs we seized documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have a look at what is contained in tab 81. Is that some kind of information coming from the Jezerce KLA staff, and what does it say?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is notification provided by Ljuftari, a solder. He is informing his staff that the inhabitants of Burnik were currently in the force because of the fighting going on in Grebnik. Grebnik is ten kilometres away from Burnik. Again, he says the Rajamine-Kacanik corridor has been cut off. This is an illegal route that the terrorists use for the transportation of firearms and other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Why did the population leave their villages? Why were they leaving, according to this document?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this document, they were leaving out of fear of possible clashes between the military and police and terrorist groups in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a notification. Notification. The original is in Albanian, it is handwritten, and a soldier who was reconnoitering informed his unit that he came across a group of inhabitants from a village. All the inhabitants of the village of Burnik, as a matter of fact, from the territory of Urosevac, and they were staying in the forest out of fear. He talked to them, and they were afraid because of the fighting going on in Grebnik, a village about ten kilometres away from Burnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are actually two informants referred to in the document, are there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second part, for Rajamine. I'm talking about Burnik now, Burnik. But the corridor had been cut off. The corridor is a road that they used and they thought was safe for transporting terrorists, materiel, and weapons between their different operative zones, and the staffs and substaffs of the terrorist units in that area. That road was cut off, Rajamine-Kacanik. The army took the area at the time, and they could not use it. So the soldier informing his unit received this information from Skender Mustafa, and the information that in the village of Plesina there were wounded soldiers. That is the territory of the municipality of Urosevac too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where does the document come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was seized after an anti-terrorist action of the KLA staff in Jezerce. According to the procedure that was then in place, every such document was sent on to the state security service along with an accompanying letter, and then they processed it further and made their own analyses. 90 per cent of the documents found in the staffs were handwritten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this refers to deportations, and you said that Albanians were fleeing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, the police that you commanded in the area of the SUP of Urosevac, how did the police behave to people who were leaving their homes?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first few days the traffic police returned these columns moving towards the border. They were sent back home. However, they tried to reach the border in any possible way. If they had set out for Djeneral Jankovic and were returned, then they would move to Globocica. That is another border post facing Macedonia. If they were returned from there, they went towards Prizren via Strpce. That was done for a few times on orders from the staff so that people would not be mistreated in any way or endangered. They could have lost their lives due to the bombing. After all, a similar thing happened during the bombing in Djakovica when a refugee column was bombed. So we stopped returning them eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You allowed them?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We could not restrict their freedom of movement. That was it. And along the road we helped them in every conceivable way; we gave them humanitarian assistance, food aid, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, were there any abuses vis-a-vis the displaced population that something unlawful or impermissible was done?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course there were individual incidents. There were cases of robbery as well. Let me give an example. We found out through operative channels that a group of reservists of the army of Yugoslavia at the border near Globocica stopped the displaced persons who were moving along and took away their money. That group was brought into custody, they were interrogated, and handed over to the military organs. They were immediately detained. These are four persons who were immediately brought into custody and handed over to the military court. We also had some cases when individual Serbs were taking buses from socially owned companies and asking individuals, civilians, for money in order to be transported. They would ask for five times as much money. Because of this, two such persons were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In those cases when they charged five times more than they were supposed to for transporting these people, is this documented in tab 82?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document contained in tab 82. There are two persons mentioned here who were detained and handed over to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. investigating judge because they mistreated citizens and abused their own authority. The judge ordered their detention, and I don't know what happened later, because on the 15th we withdrew, on the 15th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is the essence of this, the crime as described here, paragraph 1, 2, 3, 4? It says the personnel of the SUP of Urosevac were collecting information. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came to learn that through an unidentified person they found out that passengers were charged foreign currency in order to be transported on buses and five times more than they were supposed to. Should I read further on?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they could not find the reference. This is an approximate interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't speak at the same time. You're overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It also says that a record was compiled, that the money was taken away, that the person was remanded into custody, statements were taken from a number of Albanians, as you can see on page 2.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are the names of the Albanians referred to here?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, three or four names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So these are abuses. Let me not define them yet again. Do you have anything that you have to say that somebody was beating these people who were fleeing?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the territory of Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any such incidents in the territory of the SUP of Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that they weren't, because had I -- they didn't happen because had they happened, I would have been informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. These persons who were fleeing for the reasons that you mentioned, did they receive humanitarian aid from the authorities?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And practically at all the crossroads along the road there were Red Cross teams. In addition to Red Cross teams, the Civil Defence teams from the Executive Council were there, trying to persuade these persons to go back home. Sometimes they were successful, on other occasions they were not, but we worked on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid I couldn't find the reference we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I be clear about 82. 82 is about a murder or an assault, and you've told us that it was all to do with commissioning vehicles and abusing the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a second part to 82 underneath it. It may be that it's not translated. At least on mine it's not. Certainly I couldn't find the reference either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that apparently the translation provided is a completely different document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Criminal report for abuse of authority as stipulated in Article 242, paragraph 2, the Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia, falsifying official documents from Article 248, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Code of Serbia, and article 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The English document provided here has an explanation that, on the basis of murder contained in paragraph -- Article 147 -- Havzi Voglici is the name and I assume this is the person who is the victim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The interpreters have already told us that the translation relates to a completely different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For clarity and so we're all working on the same material, I've got that document the accused referred to in English. I then have something marked tab 82 and a document that is clearly longer in text than the translated document, and that document is signed by Stankovic and Trajkovic, whereas the English translation is not apparently signed by anyone. So there it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we need to get a copy of the correct version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the translation of a document that we haven't got here in Serbian, Mr. Janicevic. It says Oup-Kacanik, February 1999. This is a criminal report, again Voglici Zejdin.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably came from the group of criminal reports that had to do with Zejdin Voglici. He killed a neighbour of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who has the same last name?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, move on to 83 and let us hope that we have a correspondence in the documents there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we move on to 83, I didn't rise to object to 81, partly because a notebook of a broadly similar kind had been allowed in a previous session, but I can't really see the basis for admitting 81. It seems to me to be tenuous in the extreme, whatever it is, and I don't follow the interpretation put on the words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider that at the appropriate time. Move on to 83, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I omitted to tender these past tabs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you're tendering them now, we'll have to consider Mr. Nice's objection to 81.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what Mr. Nice's objection refers to. Mr. Janicevic explained that it is a handwritten notification, submitted on the 24th of April by a member of the KLA to his superiors. This note says that the villagers of Burnik were currently in the woods because of fighting in Grebnik and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can read the translation, but the translation indicates that it's -- it's not a soldier that's written it, it's someone commanding. The whole thing's very confusing and I, at the moment, do not understand what the document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Janicevic, I don't think it's a matter for you but for KLA, but I don't understand why they didn't -- why they had to make this kind of notification in writing, by hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that question why they did that. All I can say is that in every anti-terrorist action we came across a multitude of such documents. Every patrol coming back from a mission would write a report in longhand, in a notebook or in a special logbook. This particular note is a notification that a soldier, not a commander, not an officer but a soldier, under the pseudonym of Ljuftari, which means "warrior" in Albanian, informs his base that the villagers of Burnik were hiding in the woods from the fighting taking place in Grebnik, which is ten kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can read the document, but you have to bear in mind that Mr. Milosevic has presented to us a document and an English translation, and the English translation refers to the person who has provided the document as being a commander, 1st Battalion. Now, can you read Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can you read the very end of it, who has signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Albanian, as well, it says from a soldier. From soldier Gaustari [phoen] Ljuftari, and Ljuftari is a nickname or a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the very end of the document. What -- can you read what the very last part of it says? There's the date on the left-hand side and there's something else written on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's probably something that the Serbian translator did not manage to decipher. That's -- we see in signature all sorts of symbols, Xs. Every soldier, every terrorist had a pseudonym, a nom de guerre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Read the end part. Or can you read that part or can't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in Albanian. I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we see if this is a signature, at least?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just a signature. "KB1" and then a signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 79 and 80 we'll admit. 81 we'll not admit. 82 we'll mark for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, Mr. Robinson, why wouldn't 81 be admitted if the Serbian translator could not make out the signature? The point is in the contents, not the signature. Or do you believe the document to be less than authentic, or is there some other reason, or is the only reason that Mr. Nice says it can't be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're not satisfied about its authenticity, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, where did you get this document?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said. It was found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must move on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we have to see what happened to the English translation of 82. In the meantime, Mr. Janicevic, regarding one aspect of the charges, there is a reference to the fact that the people who were moving out as refugees had their documents seized. Can I ask you, as former chief of Urosevac SUP, what do you know about the incidence of seizure of documents from people who were crossing the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out about such claims after this indictment was brought and made public. If I had known about any such thing, I would have taken measures to stop it if indeed such a thing occurred. I would have made sure that the policemen or other officials concerned be identified and properly punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any single incident of documents, IDs being seized?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know about anything of the kind until this indictment was made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What purpose would seizure of documents have served?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that it would have served any purpose at all in any respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 63, paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear which paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 63(k).

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says that our forces attacked the villages in the municipality of Kacanik and Kacanik town itself, and that this resulted in the destruction of places of worship and houses, including but not limited to the mosques of Kotlina and Ivaja. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. I don't see how a town can be shelled by an army and the police if the army had been in that town for 50 years. There was a police station in the centre of Kacanik. Less than a kilometre away from the police station was the base of a combat group of the army. I believe the commander of the border battalion was stationed there. I don't see how they were supposed to attack themselves. They were under daily attack of the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm now talking only about 1999. To what kind of attacks were the army and the police subject to from the beginning of 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The citizens and the police in Kacanik were exposed to almost daily attacks on the road from Skopje to Pristina going via Kacanik. The road between Doganovici and Globocica. Citizens who did not agree with the terrorist policies of the KLA were kidnapped and taken away. Nobody knows where. Some of them were eventually released during anti-terrorist operations. Others were never seen again, unfortunately. In this area, it was mostly Albanians who were abducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in the majority of cases it was Albanians who were abducted.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the identity of Albanians who were abducted in Kacanik in that particular series of attacks?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I can give you examples, plus we have this list, the list of persons who had signed contracts for local security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are trying to say that it was mainly Albanians who had contracted to become local security men who were abducted.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that tab 83?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list of persons who had signed the contract for local security for Kacanik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2nd November 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What else do we see?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Name, number of uniform, personal sidearm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the next list?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a list of persons who had applied to become local security men in the municipality of Kacanik while not having weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have an English translation here. I don't know if you do. Maybe it was simply omitted from my binder.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, do you have an English translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we have. We have an English translation of -- is this 83?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the first list contains 38 names, bears the seal and signature of the president of the Municipal Council. Thirty-eight persons, with the number of their uniform indicated and type of weapon carried. And the other list is dated 26th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there are some persons who, in the meantime, had been issued with weapons. There's only one exception; Agim Idrizi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, you explained that the allegation in paragraph (k) was to be questioned because Kacanik was already occupied by Serb forces and therefore for that reason it was unlikely that Serb forces would attack Kacanik. I have heard that explanation before, but it's not clear to me exactly what is meant by that. If Serb forces are in Kacanik and they're in a particular location, why would it not be possible for the Serbs to attack the village nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm -- I hope you don't mind my saying so, but can I ask you how can Serb forces attack a town in whose centre they are located themselves, which they patrol every day, every day, day and night? A town that, until the end of the war, had never been held by the terrorists. There were several attempts by the terrorists to take over the town, to seize the police station, to expel the army from those positions, but they were unsuccessful. There were a number of attacks, terrorists attacks, on the army and the police. Why would police forces attack the town if they are already holding it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They're already in occupation, so there would be no need for them to attack the town. That's what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not use the word "occupation," but if somebody is stationed in a town for 50 years, doing their job, it's not occupation. They're in their own town. It's not an occupation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a very specific question: Was Kacanik under the control of our forces throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Our forces handed over the town to the KFOR under the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So throughout the war, Kacanik was under the control of our forces?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is all of Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole of the town of Kacanik, yes, was under our control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, could you explain to us this second list which was signed -- actually, it was sent to the Secretariat of the Interior, to the head of the Urosevac SUP; is that right? That's you.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was signed by an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what does it say on the stamp? You have it in Serbian and Albanian. On the stamp itself, what does it say there?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosovo Democratic Initiative. That is a party of Albanians with headquarters or the Municipal Board in Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the president of the party?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Seljim Topojani, and his deputy was Saip Reka, but unfortunately, both of them were kidnapped and killed in a very brutal manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he drew up a list and sent it to you of individuals who reported to do local security work and had no weapons and expected to be issued them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just to make that clear. On the first list we have some 38 names and on the second list 17 names, which makes it a total of 55 persons. Were they -- did they mostly fall casualty?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty-one of them were kidnapped, the fate is ten is not known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Mr. Robinson, I'd like to tender tab 83. May it be exhibited, both these lists?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, did the SUP of Urosevac take any steps to uncover the kidnapped Albanians, to find them, and the perpetrators of these crimes? Did they take any steps to do that?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After every report of kidnapping, the SUP of Urosevac went out in the field to check it out and took steps to uncover what had happened. On the 27th of February, 1999, a person was kidnapped, an activist of the party, in fact, and his name was Riza Kiki, and he was a member of the local security, too, in the village of Gajre. The commander of the police station in Kacanik, the late Bogoljub Sajetovic [phoen], who was a police captain, was called up on the phone by the terrorists and informed that Riza Kiki had been kidnapped and that he would be killed. Now, he went out to check this out in the village of Gajre, which is two and a half kilometres away from Kacanik, to the house there, and he was -- there was an ambush set up in a stream, and he and the patrol that was with him were shot at from and hand-held rocket launcher, from automatic rifles, and he was killed on the spot. In addition to him, four policemen were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he went to look for the kidnapped Albanian, having received Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. information over the phone, he was caught in an ambush and lost his life there, and three other policemen were wounded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in this -- was the staff of the MUP in Pristina and the Kosovo Verification Mission informed about that event?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kosovo Information Mission -- or Verification Mission was informed before us about the kidnapping of Riza Kiki, before us, and they came to the police station to check out the validity of the information they had received, and they -- the commanding officer offered that they could go together and check out the situation. It was a Sunday, I believe, but they refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they arrived. He offered, Srdemovic [phoen] offered that they could go out and check the situation out together, and they refused. And had they gone, they would have been caught in the ambush.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, had they gone maybe they would not have been -- there would not have been an ambush, but I assume there would have been nonetheless. But otherwise, in every terrorist action and police action undertaken, either to apprehend the perpetrators of a crime or any violations or misdemeanors that had been carried out, or pursuant to a court order, the Verification Mission was informed of all these matters, and they had their department in Kacanik, their office in Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what operation was this?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an operative action to check out the information received by telephone to see if it was true or not. And after that, they went in search of the terrorist group and learnt that the group had put up in the village of Ivaja, that that was where the Main Staff of the 162nd Brigade was located, that they had a substaff in the village of Kotlina with about 70 members, in the village of Pustenik as well, Palivodenica, and several other villages in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was undertaken to find and apprehend the people who, from the beginning of the NATO aggression, launched attacks on civilian police and military features in Kacanik, in Kacanik and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Measures were taken to find them and apprehend them, together with the border battalion of the army, since most of the Kacanik municipality lies along the border belt. The police went out in search of the terrorists. Sometimes it was successful, sometimes not, but it didn't stop its search until the 24th of March, that is to say the first day the bombing started. Some of the people who had been kidnapped in those anti-terrorist actions were liberated. They were freed. However, the terrorists were successful in taking some of these to other places and all trace is lost of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that Kacanik was under the control of our forces throughout. You explained that to us. Now, can you give us an explanation with relation to a detail in count 63(k), paragraph 63(k), where it says allegedly that, in addition to our attacks in Kacanik, that houses and religious sites were destroyed in Kotlina and Ivaja.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that the houses were destroyed and the mosques in Kotlina and Ivaja. In the village of Ivaja, for example - and I've repeated it several times - is where the headquarters and staff of the 162nd Terrorist Brigade was located. And in the other village, there was the substaff, numbering about 80 people. In the search to apprehend the terrorists, the joint forces of the army and the police dealt with Ivaja first and then Kotlina in this anti-terrorist operation. And the last time they entered Kotlina, on the 24th of March, as I was informed, there was an attack. As the army and police passed through the village, there was an attack launched on them from a hill where there was a bunker, and a group of terrorists came out of the bunker and shot at the police and army members in the back. After that, the terrorists were surrounded and in combat they were killed. The bunker was the size of -- or, rather, it was about 4 by 8 metres. There were two bunkers, in fact, two entrances to a bunker, one horizontal and one lateral, and 50 metres away there was a corridor that had been dug out, and according to my technicians, about 200 members of the terrorist organisation could be accommodated in that corridor dugout.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the 24th of March. Look at what it says in paragraph 63(i).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us anything about the destruction of the mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no destruction of the mosques. Had there been any, I would certainly have been informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 63(i), it says that: "On or about the 8th of March, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked and partially burnt the village of Kotlina. On the 24th of March, 1999 -" that's the date you just mentioned - "they attacked Kotlina again with heavy weapon systems and soldiers. Many of the male residents of Kotlina fled into nearby forests during this attack while the forces of the FRY and Serbia ordered the women, children, and elderly to board trucks which took them towards the town of Kacanik. Those who could not fit into the trucks were compelled to walk behind them towards Kacanik. A number of male residents of Kotlina were killed during this attack, including at least 17 men whose bodies were thrown into wells. Before departing Kotlina, forces of the FRY and Serbia burnt the remainder of the village." Is any of what I've just read out to you true, or are parts of it true or what?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of that is true. First of all, on the 8th of March, the verifiers followed the entire operation both in Kotlina and Ivaja. After that operation, I talked to the verifiers and they never, not at any single point did they make any complaints or say that there had been destruction in Kotlina and Ivaja. They told us that in the village of Kotlina they were -- the population was fleeing, fled away and could the population go back to their village? I said they could because it was their village and their houses. There was no mention at all of a single house being set fire to. And there were four of them, four verifiers. I can't remember their names, although we do have the names in our report. On the 24th of March, there were no verifiers there. The population -- or, rather, I explained a moment ago what happened, how the event unfolded; they attacked the police and army from the rear, from their backs. They came out of the bunker, they were surrounded and lost their lives in the fighting. As I was informed, there were not 17 but in fact 22 persons, 22 terrorists, and the list says 17. There was an on-site investigation conducted, a set of photographs was established, and the investigating judge went out on the spot. Everything was documented. The population, the inhabitants who had fled were fleeing as of the 8th of March and even before. They took to the forests, and they went down a slope to reach the railway line and the Skopje Kacanik communication line or road. And they were hungry and tired, and that's how they came out onto the road. And my policemen gave the people their own lunch packets. In talking to the citizens, and there's documents -- there are documents to bear that out, it says that the terrorists forced them out of their homes and forced them to flee and take to the forest, to show that this was a humanitarian catastrophe, to portray it as such. And I say that with full responsibility. They waited for them, they took them to Kacanik, they put them up in the cultural centre there, together with representatives of the Red Cross and the Civil Defence staff. They gave them food and clothing, and after that, the people went off where they wanted to go. Most of them went back to their village, the village that they had come from in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this information that was provided to you, information that the terrorists forced the villagers to flee; and if so, who provided that information to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there is an Official Note and report in the documents, and the interviews conducted with the villagers of Kotlina and the other village, I think it was called Pustenik. So every village in that border belt had an occasion where the population took to the forests and fled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm asking, how did you come by that information? Is it from reading the reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the citizens. Yes, I read reports from my officers based on the statements taken from the citizens of Kotlina -- or, rather, villagers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Some wells are mentioned here. Let me just tell you that we didn't provide all these photographs here, but we provided them when Obrad Stevanovic testified about Kotlina, and I assume you're mentioning the photo documents there because it was your Urosevac SUP that took them. Now, what wells are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained this a moment ago. There weren't any wells. I don't think anybody would be mad to dig a well on the top of a hill. That's the first point. Secondly, they were specially made bunkers. One had not been completed, its construction wasn't finished. It had -- it lacked a covering, a cover. But I have some photographs here showing those so-called wells, if you would like to take a look at them on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Put them on the overhead projector. Let's take a look at them. Let's go through them very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the so-called wells.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is one of the horizontal entrances to that so-called well. There was a vertical one and then they made a horizontal entrance, and that's the entrance here. Beside the entrance was one of the terrorists who was killed. There's another one over here. I think that so far in my practice in the police force, my experience, I never came across anybody putting a furnace, a tin furnace, in a well. This is the tin furnace that has burnt down, and that tin furnace was in the bunker which the terrorists used for heating when it was cold. Now, this is the civilian, the person they say is a civilian. You can part of a uniform and boots. Here is another photograph, showing a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... if we're supposed to make sense of it, I suppose we ought to look at it and see what the witness is pointing to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You'd like to see it a little more, Mr. Nice, is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I now see what he's pointing to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When would this photograph have been taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That civilian -- they were taken on the 24th of March in the afternoon hours after the terrorist operation had concluded. In 1999, of course. Parts of the uniform. This is the lower half, and army boots, and a rifle next to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And whose body are we looking at? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. An unidentified terrorist, or at least I don't know his name, nor did we -- nor were we able to identify him at that time. The original photographic material already exists in Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So your reference to so-called wells is to indicate what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that they weren't wells at all, that they were bunkers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He says that this original photographic material exists in the Court. I think he's probably correct because I recognise one of those photographs as having been displayed before, but perhaps the accused could tell us what the exhibit number is so that I can dig it out and have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, can you assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The cross-reference says that tab 84 and 85 are tab 212 of 299.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may remove it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this first part of paragraph 63, it says that on the 8th of March, our forces attacked the village on the 8th of March and partially burned it. You just mentioned that that was the date when the KVM was there.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The verifiers were practically in the field with the police and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just add one more thing. On the 8th of March, there were five vehicles of the Verification Mission in Kotlina after the action. Five vehicles, with two verifiers in every one of them, that makes a total of ten. So ten verifiers did not see that the village was destroyed, that the mosques were destroyed, everything else that is contained in this paragraph. Now, I really don't know how this came to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What about the bodies of the -- thrown into the wells? You explained that these were not wells.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're not wells, and they were not thrown in. After carrying out the on-site investigation, when night fell, the investigation team withdrew, together with the forces that were in the sector. The population that went down to the road and the railway was transferred to Kacanik and put up at the cultural centre. Others went to stay with relatives or friends. They were taken care of. Those who needed medical assistance were taken to the health centre because it is close to the cultural centre. And practically there were no objections raised. A group of about 20 persons was brought into custody. They were suspected of being terrorists, judging by the way they looked and the uniforms they had. In the meantime, they had thrown their weapons away. The paraffin glove test was applied to all of them. All the tests were positive. Not a single person was detained. They were all released so that we would not cause any kind of dissatisfaction among the members of the Albanian community in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Or, rather, you established that they had been shooting and you nevertheless released them, let them go home?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We thought that they would stay with their families and that they would not return to the terrorist groups that were in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Partial documentation in relation to what we've been saying just now about Kotlina, is it contained in tabs 84 and 85? Please look at tab 84 and 85. This is a document that was compiled on the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Photo documentation is being provided.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the investigating judge of the municipal court in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the crime of terrorism in the village of Kotlina, municipality of Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you can see who received it and when.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then there is a list.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And a complete list of the photo documentation contained and all the objects found on site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And then tab 85 refers to photo documentation from Ivaja, or was it Kotlina? No, this is the village of Kotlina. Kotlina. And then it says Ivaja in brackets.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photo documentation was both for Kotlina and Ivaja. The first part is Ivaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I can see, the first part is the staff of Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Kotlina, Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These two tabs appear to be confused in the copies we have. There's a list of what they're supposed to be in number 84, but the photographs generally appear to be in 85.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Black and white photographs, not in colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The -- the picture which appears in the middle of the fourth page, is it not the picture we saw just now, the original one you showed us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And these two tabs are as I noted, tab 212 of D299. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at photograph 19. Even without a translation provided, it will be easy for you to see what it is. Indeed, you can see the entrance here into this facility that looks like a well.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Underneath is a photograph with some steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you can see a ladder on photograph 20, the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was -- is this the weapons that were seized in the area?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is also something that's in colour here towards the end, towards the end of this tab 85. A few moments ago we couldn't see them properly.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether you have these colour photographs, gentlemen, at the end of tab 85.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we have two pages of colour and one black and white.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have several pages of photographs in black and white and three of colour photographs. It's probably -- all of this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's quite confusing. You get a lot of help from everybody in this Court, but you must sort this one out yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have my colour version now from Ms. Dicklich, for which I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I could check in the break as to precisely what has been exhibited before, because it seems that there may be new photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the members of the Urosevac SUP interview the inhabitants of the Kotlina and Ivaja? If they did, what did they learn; and if they didn't, just say no.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did interview the inhabitants of Ivaja and Kotlina, and what they learned from them is what I referred to a few moments ago, that the terrorists had forced them to flee into the forests.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... we're going to be privileged to see or is this just coming in the form of oral hearsay?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this cannot be information based on rumours because it is the chief of the Secretariat of the Ministry of the Interior who is testifying here, or, if you want to use your own vocabulary, the chief of police in that area. So he is not talking about rumours. He is talking about information that he learned in the course of carrying out his duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If he's able to, he should provide the source of the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, you heard Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source of information are Official Notes and statements that were collected by my employees from the citizens of Ivaja and Kotlina on the 8th of March and the 24th of March, after the anti-terrorist actions were brought to an end. I think or -- rather, I'm sure that these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. statements are contained in that first group of tabs, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which ones are that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first binder. The first or the second binder, I'm not too sure. Would you like me to look it up during the break so that I don't keep you any longer now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Find it for us in the break. Mr. Nice will be interested in that, no doubt. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 10:56 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I attempt to clarify tabs 84 and 85.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If you go first of all to tab 84, the first page is in fact D299, tab 211, and the rest is D299 tab 212. In tab 84, you will see that there is a list, quite a difficult list to read, which looks like this, if I can show for Your Honours' assistance. It's a faint list which has S1 to S26, and that is a list for the black and white photo set that is in tab 85. Have Your Honours located that? The second page, which is also a list, 1 to 31, appears to be the list of equipment, a translation of which we have further on in tab 84. If we then turn to tab 85, the first eight pages of black and white photographs are already exhibited as D299, tab 212. After the first eight pages, Your Honours should have a list, which is -- I have in my bundle a list 1 to 31 again, which is an equipment list repeat. There is a final black and white photo at the end of your bundle, two photos, which very faintly looks as if it says S1.something 5. From our research, these photographs, two photographs, have not been exhibited before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we have the two pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: One. I think we have one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two black and white photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They're the first of the black and white photos on mine. Is that them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Those two photographs have not been previously admitted. And then we come to the first colour photograph, which has been shown on the ELMO. The first colour set of photographs, the first page, is actually a colour set of the black and white which you already have, and it's the last three colour photos that are new. In my submission, it may be more prudent that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do the last three look like? My last group is four.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And this one. So those three are the new photographs, along with the one I've just referred to, the last black and white. For the sake of prudence, it might be better, I would submit, to just allow the photographs to come in, having most of them been admitted, but it may be better to tie up with the materials that are already in the file for the sake of ease of reference later on for analysis purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Higgins. We'll admit 85 as one exhibit, as Ms. Higgins has suggested, including the colour photographs. I thought 84 had already been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, 84 is already admitted as tab 211 and tab 212 of Exhibit 299.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, I understood you to say, and I may have misunderstood, but there are two lists of equipment in tab 84, and you didn't indicate that either of these had been admitted already, did you?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If I can just clarify that, Your Honour. In tab 84 there is a list of equipment which has previously been admitted. It is D299, tab 212. The only clarification I sought to give you was that the first page of that is incorrectly indexed. It is, in fact, D299, tab 211.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have now received a translation of tab 82. So that will now be admitted. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I won't go back to tab 82, because I got the translation that you got just now and that you admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, in relation to the question pertaining to interviews about what happened in Ivaja and Kotlina, you mentioned that in your records you had some documents indicating these interviews. Did you manage to find any of them during the break?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found three statements, because I had very little time. One is 18.11. So it is tab 18.11, Ljuta Berat, who claims that "... on the 7th of March, 1999 -" that is a day before the anti-terrorist action in Ivaja started - "around 2100 hours when we villagers of Ivaja, municipality of Kacanik, left our houses with our families and in the woods between Ivaja village and Ljaci neighbourhood I met forester..." so-and-so, and then he says what he talked about to him. That is a day before the anti-terrorist action. So that is one such statement. There is tens of them, but I didn't have time to look them all up now. Let me indicate some more. One more: Hoxha Islam is the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What tab?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean 18.25?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He says that on the 28th he went to see his father-in-law in Gajre, on the 28th of February, that is, and he explains what he saw there. It's somewhere towards the middle of the page. I don't know which paragraph it is. I underlined it. Should I read it out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record it's not 18.25. It's just tab 25.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I'm so sorry. It is tab 25. Somewhere just below the middle, he says that before the anti-terrorist operation he ran into the station commander in Gajre. He talked to him, and he says that they told him that the police were coming. And when he came to the yard of his father-in-law, the father-in-law was already getting ready to leave the house, and together with the father-in-law and all the other villagers, he went to the woods before the anti-terrorist operation was carried out, the one in which Bogoljub Sajetovic was killed. So that's in tab 25, somewhere in the middle of the text. And I found another one which is a record on taking a statement, tab 26. Abazi Camil gave the statement. That is the document in which it was disputed who exactly signed the statement on behalf of authorised officials. He says in the beginning of the statement, starting with: "Ten days ago, or more precisely on the 26th of February, 1999, together with my family and other villagers of Ljac hamlet, Pustenik village, Kacanik municipality, we organised a column of refugees, following orders of Acif Ljaci, representative of our hamlet, out of fear because in the immediate vicinity of our hamlet several artillery shells had exploded. Acif Ljaci later became commander of the KLA for the village of Pustenik." We can see that clearly from this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is in the statement? What you just said is part of the statement or is it just evidence that you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's part the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a translation of tab 26 in English? There isn't one in my text. Okay. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, you have explained that a number of people, based on the information you had collected, were brought in for interrogation and were later, all of them, released.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. If I may add one more thing. In tab 25, on page number 2, or maybe page number 3, one page seems to be missing, it says: "That night, OSCE representatives told the villagers of Gajre to leave the village and go to Bob village or to Kacanik because the police would come to maltreat and beat innocent villagers.
