Following orders of OSCE representatives, the villagers of Gajre left the village the same night and went to Bob village, Kacanik municipality, where I went, too, with my family." That is a statement by Islam Hoxha.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue, Mr. Robinson? Can we move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, in paragraph 63(ii) it says: "On the 27th and 28th of March, forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked the town of Kacanik. They harassed, detained, beat, and shot many Kosovo Albanian residents of Kacanik, as a result of which thousands of persons fled to nearby forests and eventually walked across the border into Macedonia. Other persons, other displaced persons from the town of Kacanik and nearby villages walked to the village of Stagovo where they boarded trains that took them to the Macedonian border." You don't have to repeat the explanation that Kacanik was under our control throughout that time. I'm interested in the latter part of this paragraph concerning the village of Stagovo and the claim that these displaced persons walked to Macedonia. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This assertion makes no sense at all. Stagovo is closer to the central part of Kosovo, closer to Urosevac. Kacanik has a police station, and it's 30 kilometres away from the Djeneral Jankovic crossing, through the gorge. I don't know why they would take that route to the border. That is a very long way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this shooting in Kacanik, the shooting of the citizens and the expulsion of civilians?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can claim with full responsibility that there was no shooting of citizens in Kacanik. There was no shooting as such. I know that. I would have known about it if there had been any, and of course I would have taken appropriate measures against offenders, but it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did the police station in Kacanik work throughout the war? Did they perform their regular duties?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 12th of June, 1999, the police station in Kacanik operated and so did the section of internal affairs. On the 10th of June, we carried out an on-site investigation in the killing of two Macedonians near Skopje. It was performed by the team that went out from Kacanik town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Janicevic, if all these allegations are untrue, then why did the citizens of Kacanik leave their homes at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just spoke about the killing of Mahmut Daliste and his neighbour Reka Camil. Their bodies were held for two days in the yard of a house in Rakovac mahala to intimidate the other residents, to show them that whoever is not with them is against them. Second, they spread rumours that NATO would make a ground invasion just in the area of Kacanik. Many of my neighbours asked me if this information was true. I'm sorry I didn't tell them that it was true, because they would be alive today. As it were, they were brutally killed as soon as NATO came into the area of Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want to return to the -- this question of Kacanik being under the control of the Serb forces, thereby making it unlikely that Serb forces would attack Kacanik. Is it Kacanik the town that was under the control of Serb forces, as distinct from the municipality of Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. The town of Kacanik was under the absolute control of Serb forces, both the police and the army, while terrorist forces were stationed in certain villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In paragraph (k) of the indictment, that is 63(k), Mr. Milosevic, the allegation is that forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked villages in the Kacanik municipality and the town of Kacanik itself. So, Mr. Janicevic, the explanation that you gave that Kacanik was under Serb control, that would apply to the town but not necessarily to the villages in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, most villages in the area of Kacanik municipality were under the control of Serb forces. Until the 28th of February, 1999, the police freely entered any village in the area of Kacanik municipality. Any village. I claim this with full responsibility. Reckoning that there were going to be no problems, and there were indeed no problems until the 28th, 28th of February, 1999, the police went into this village to check the situation, and that's why two policemen were killed. Things later deteriorated. The police and the army did not have any reason to attack villages inhabited by Albanians. Albanians were at the time citizens of Yugoslavia, and nowadays Serbia and Montenegro. I hope they are still the citizens of that country. Nobody had any reason to fear the army or the police. They were fleeing from fighting and from the terrorists. Those who did not accept their ideas had no hope of living to see the morrow. I'm telling you, many of my friends met their end in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A very specific question: Were there any cases of expulsion of Albanians in that area?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not on the part of the police or the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janicevic. Paragraph 63(iv), it says: "On or about 25 May 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked the village of Dubrava in the municipality of Kacanik. During the attack, forces of the FRY and Serbia killed several Kosovo Albanian residents of Dubrava. Many residents of Dubrava formed a convoy of tractors and trailers and fled to Macedonia. Other residents fled to other villages or into forests before eventually crossing the border into Macedonia." Do you know anything about this incident that allegedly occurred on the 25th of May; that is, an attack on the village of Dubrava, the killing of several residents - it says several Kosovo Albanians here - and the death of many others?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that there was any killing. Some people may have got killed in the fighting. Every day we had a dozen terrorists attacks in that area. The road to Tetovo and Globocica passes by Dubrava. An hour would not pass without an attack on a police patrol, an army patrol, a transport convoy, customs officers, civilians. In the last few days of the war, an hour would not pass in peace. I don't see how the police could attack. They had to defend themselves, though. If they hadn't defended themselves, that would have been quite good for the terrorists, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, 66(l) says that: "From March to May 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia launched a series of massive offensives against several villages in the municipality of Kacanik, which resulted in the deaths of more than 100 civilians."

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is nonsense. The truth is that there are 93 people killed, and this photograph is to be found in the shop window of a photo studio in Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 86 shows this collective photo of members of the KLA of the 162nd Brigade who were killed while fighting our forces. Very well. Mr. Robinson, I would like to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, tell us now briefly what you know about the consequences of the NATO bombing at civilian features in the Urosevac SUP area, the Stimlje Kacanik, Strpce municipalities and Urosevac municipality.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and remember all the details of that. In Strpce, for example, two repeaters of the RTS were destroyed. At least that's one and another one. In the Kacanik area, the PTT cross-section, very important for the whole area and the south of the Balkans, and also another thing that was bombed was the Simpo factory, the administrative building of the factory. In the Urosevac area, near the agricultural airport, where there were hangars belonging to the factory farm, they were completely destroyed, and an FM repeat -- transmitter was bombed, and during the bombing there was a lot of damage to houses in the village of Varos, which is close by, close by the airport, the agricultural airport. In Staro Selo, several houses were damaged and the Orthodox cemetery was almost completely destroyed under the NATO bombing. In Urosevac on a number of occasions bombs attacked a 110-kilowatt power station, transformer station, which led to serious material damage. In Stimlje, at the entrance to Stimlje and Brnac [phoen] two bombs fell which destroyed a number of private dwellings. In Urosevac a bomb fell within the factory producing pipes, and a large part of the settlement and some Albanian houses were destroyed, Albanian houses bordering on the factory compound, and seven or eight persons were injured. I'm not quite sure of the exact number. I apologise if I've got the number wrong. In the village of Donja Batina, another bomb fell. That is also the Strpce area, general area of Strpce, and some ten houses were damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you going to relate through this witness the effects of the bombing to the charges in the indictment? You must relate it to your case and to the Prosecution case. And as I understand it, it may be relevant in terms of persons fleeing. It may also be relevant in terms of your contention that there was collaboration between NATO and the UCK. The point I'm making is that this case is not about NATO bombing and the effects. You should try to relate it to the case that you're presenting in your Defence, to show that either people fled because of the bombing and not because, as is alleged in the indictment, of the crimes committed by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has double importance, a twofold importance, Mr. Robinson. First of all, on the basis of what the witness has just said with respect to the NATO bombing, we can see that there was mass bombing, and certainly anybody with any reason can assume that people fled in the face of it. And secondly, during the bombing, the witness mentioned several examples of how the houses were damaged, too, houses belonging to the population. And what Mr. Nice says, this is ascribed to destruction by Serb forces and FRY forces. So on the one hand we have bombing as the reason for which people fled, and on the other hand, as a consequence of the bombing, we have the destruction of a large number of features which otherwise are ascribed to the forces of the FRY and Serbia, and they never shelled any villages, they just engaged in combat against terrorists, and that is what the witness said on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You will be relating this to specific charges in the indictment. That's my point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's related to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not through this witness but through some other witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think through this witness as well, because all these places are mentioned in what Mr. Nice likes to call an indictment, and the destruction of houses quite obviously represents the consequence of the NATO bombing. The fleeing of the population also is a consequence of NATO's bombing, and the witness has been speaking about the extent of the activity and the aggression against my country, the extent of it, which caused these consequences and results. And this activity brings such consequences all over our planet, all over the globe. Where there is bombing, civilians flee. Where there is bombing, houses are destroyed, houses are burning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it is a matter for you how you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. present your Defence, but if I were representing your Defence, I would attempt to be a little more specific and try to relate it to charges in the indictment. As it is, if you merely say that there was mass bombing, then -- and you lead no evidence specifically to show that persons fled because of the bombing, you would be left in your address to merely put to the Chamber what you are just putting without any specific evidence from persons to say that they fled because of the indictment. You will raise it as an argument in your address or in your written submissions, but there won't be any sound evidential basis. Proceed. You will be asking us to infer from what you call the mass bombings that persons fled because you say it's reasonable. Any reasonable person would know that persons would flee if their villages are bombed, but your case would be much stronger if you're able to show that through -- through evidence, through the evidence of witnesses. And similarly, you say that the bombing is important also because destruction which the indictment attributes to Serb forces is properly the result of that bombing. That has to be addressed in more specific terms.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand, Mr. Robinson, how I can be more specific when we have a witness here who is speaking about his own area, his own Secretariat of the Interior, Urosevac, Stimlje, and Strpce municipalities. Here we have Urosevac, Stimlje, and Kacanik, and they have been quoted in the indictment as places where some sort of crimes on the part of the FRY forces and Serbia were committed, and he said that none of that was true and he explained what was true and correct. So I'm asking him now what is correct. He's explaining that none of it is correct. I'm asking whether he knows anything about the NATO bombing, and he's telling us what he knows about the NATO bombing. Whether there was expulsion of the population, he claims there was not. Whether the object was to kill a civilian, he claims it was not. And that's what I claim too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a single -- was there a case in the village of Doganovic where a group of children were killed from the results of cluster bombs?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Five children of Albanian ethnicity were killed, I think it was the month of May, from cluster bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Stop there. Is there an allegation in the indictment that these five persons were killed by Serb forces? This may be an illustration of the approach that you are taking. Otherwise, what is the importance of this evidence that five children were killed by -- by the bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the indictment there's very little mention of children, but they are in fact mentioned in several places, child casualties. Here we have a specific event where they were killed -- where children were killed by NATO bombs. I don't see that there were not children killed in some other incidents, too, but if you look at all the numbers in Kosovo, then it's easy to establish the ratio between the terrorists arrested who were released after the war and those who lost their lives in clashes with the forces of the army of Yugoslavia and police, et cetera. And you'll be able to draw your own conclusions just looking at the figures whether it was an intent to throw -- expulse anyone, or kill them or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, how did the NATO aggression affect our country, its organisation, weapons, the KLA forces, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not a proper question to put to the witness, how did the aggression --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm encouraging you, Mr. Milosevic, to do something other than present a broad picture of the situation. The more specific you can, then you should be.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll be quite specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, take a look at tab 87, now, please, if you would. Is that a document of the KLA, the operative zone, Nerodimlje operation zone, or tell us what it says in the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosovo liberation army, Nerodimlje operation zone, 161st Ahmet Kaciku Brigade number 184, date the 29th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is four days after the beginning of the aggression; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, read what it says next. It says: "To the 1st Battalion ..."

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To the 1st Battalion, in view of the circumstances that have arisen and on seeing the order of the ZON command, the following order is hereby issued. Order: Ordering all battalion and company commanders, companies, that is my company commander, 1, to assume a high state of readiness this evening, the 29th of March, 1999, from the moment this order is received. "Number 2: To position soldiers on the hilltops surrounding the territory they control. "3: This order is issued because we know that an air drop is expected. "4: Everything happening in the field (amounts, locations, et cetera) should be reported to your command and our command."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, and the date is Malopoljce 29th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the brigade commander signed it and his pseudonym was Granit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the original of the order that we have. We have it in Albanian. And the number was the 29th of March of the 161st Brigade. What does this order tell you?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order tells us about the cooperation between NATO forces in the air and terrorist forces on the ground. And this indicates that the terrorists were the infantry of the NATO Air Force in that area, in that region. And on several occasions we received intelligence that they were being given assistance from the air, in the air of Jezerce and the mountains around there, from Budakovo to Malopoljce, Racak, et cetera. During the night mostly, air drops during the night containing ammunition, weapons, and other combat equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, in addition to this, the air drops, NATO air drops to the KLA, was there any other form of assistance? Do you know of any other form of assistance that came in from abroad? Don't give us any general answers, try and give general answers, just specifically.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that volunteers came from America, for example. I know that there was material aid and assistance sent across land and from the air, as we said, illegally into the country, and sometimes at legal border crossing points under different documents. But there were a lot of volunteers coming in from America. American citizens, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you come to know that?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that on the basis of intelligence received. And also in Jezerce we found a list, a piece of paper, where it says what was issued to soldiers coming in from America.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that to be found in tab 88?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, because it says, "For soldiers from America." It's a notebook and it says, "For soldiers from America."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then we have it written in hand, the handwritten list, and then we have the translation typed out on a typewriter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... this and the previous exhibit to know where they come from. I can always deal with it in cross-examination but the earlier the better, as far as I'm concerned. Translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, where does this order come from, this 161st Brigade in tab 87 that you commented on a moment ago and this handwritten list for soldiers from America?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the staff of the 161st Brigade of the KLA in Jezerce. It was seized during the last anti-terrorist operation in 1999 and handed over to the staff and headquarters of MUP or, rather, the state security department from which it was obtained pursuant to a request made by your legal associates - Momo Raicevic, in actual fact - along with some more documents that have not been attached here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I should like to tender tabs 87 and 88 into evidence, please, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, they are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is no translation of 87, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is no translation of 87, so that is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have a translation of 87. There's no translation of 88, and I don't think the witness dealt with the provenance of 88 either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us return to 88, Mr. Milosevic. Elicit from the witness evidence about the provenance of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, have I understood that properly? Tab 87 has a translation, and it has been exhibited, is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. And that's the one where we see the order to position soldiers on hilltops, expecting an air drop. Now, tab 88, written in handwriting, is a document written for soldiers from America.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you get that piece of paper from?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was found in notebook 13, as it says here in the translation. It says in notebook 13, and it was seized during the anti-terrorist organisation from the staff headquarters in 1999 and sent to the state security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where was the document found?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Jezerce, the staff of the 161st Brigade in Jezerce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there an anti-terrorist operation launched then when this was seized?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will that do, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's meaningless at the moment. I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can he take it any further, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the core of the matter is that this document pertains to soldiers from America, and further on it says what was being provided in terms of what they needed; salt, cigarettes, tins, blankets, sponges, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Forty cartons of cigarettes, 55 kilogrammes of salt, ten kilogrammes of sugar, five litres of oil, eight --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There's 15 items, 15 different items, supplies needed by soldiers from America.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first page, which is typewritten, is a different document from the second page, which is in handwriting, and I don't see anything in this document which says these are part of seized documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, the original seized document is handwritten, and it includes only the page that pertains to soldiers from America. The rest was not included pertaining to soldiers, as they call them, from other groups. So as far as the original document is concerned, only that page has been included, the page that pertains to the soldiers from America. And in the translation it only says what is included as a whole in that list. So it is not a verbatim translation of everything that is written on that page. It's just a summary, sort of, of what the original page says, and it pertains to soldiers from America only. The point of introducing this document is the fact that soldiers came from America and what they got for them. We're not interested in the rest, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, is there a basis for the admission of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very difficult to say without there being, of course, a translation to work out the difference between the two documents. Perhaps the best course would be to mark it for identification until we're able to see the meaning of the document. Clearly, if it pertains to supplies being given to Americans and if there is on the face of the document, we know the witness says it was seized from an anti-terrorist operation, it may well be that it's relevant. It's hard to say at this stage. I would submit that it should be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we'll mark it for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, since you spent your entire career in Kosovo, can you tell us in one sentence only, please, if possible, what was the basic objective of the terrorists over all those years?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic objective of the terrorists --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I listened to the last compendious question, it rather looks like the flourish that Your Honour, His Honour Judge Robinson, sees as the herald of the conclusion of examination-in-chief, and I think probably a fairly offensive type of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I missed it. Mr. Milosevic, I'm not allowing that question it's -- [Microphone not activated] -- relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. If it's not relevant, if the general question will not do, then I'll put it very specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, please look at tab 89. What does tab 89 contain?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 89 contains a military oath of the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And what does this military oath say? You have the translation.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "Military oath."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Name, father's name, et cetera. And then what does it say? "As a member of the KLA ..."

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... I swear that I will fight for the liberation of the occupied Albanian lands and their unification --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "-- that I will always be a devoted fighter --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if there is a specific question, then put it, but we have the oath translated here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I put the specific question of what the objective of the terrorists was, based on the experience of Mr. Janicevic who spent his entire career there. Here in the oath, it says to liberate occupied Albanian lands and to unify them. So I'm asking

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of occupied Albanian lands does this actually refer to, Mr. Janicevic?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are no occupied lands. This is specifically Kosovo, Macedonia, Western Macedonia, Northern Greece, and part of Montenegro, which, according to the plans dating to the Prizren League in 1878, are territories that Albanians aspire to take or, rather, to create a Greater Albania in the area. Ethnically pure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's as far as the Serbs are concerned. And what was their objective vis-a-vis their own countrymen?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their own countrymen? Those who did not support their ideas did not belong to Kosovo, or could not stay alive, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... seems to be a general point and not based on this document. I'm not sure upon what it is based. It's a matter for the Court whether they want to hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have the oath here and it shows us the general aims and aspirations of the KLA. It doesn't seem to me that this witness can take it any further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I wanted to do, to ask for it to be admitted into evidence. The question I put to him just now has to do with the next document that is contained in tab 90. Mr. Robinson, have you admitted the previous document, document 89?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, military oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is contained in tab 90? Are Albanians referred to here or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Albanians only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please read the second paragraph. It is the Main Staff of the Liberation Army of Kosovo, headed by --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the KLA, headed by Mr. Jakup Krasniqi stated that an investigation should be carried out concerning three persons. The first is Ramadan Sermagja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is he an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is a member of the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You don't have to read on. And who is this next one, Ruzhdi Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also an Albanian who allegedly reported that a countryman of his possessed a revolver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the third one on that page?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third one is also an Albanian, Sinan Lakna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be admitted as well? Admitted into evidence, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this and the source?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What's the source of this document, Mr. Janicevic?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source is the same as for the previous documents that were in the Albanian language; that is to say, it was found after an anti-terrorist action in Jezerce at the KLA headquarters there in 1999. It was submitted to the state security sector, and at the request of your legal associates, it was received from them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance lies in the fact that this is just one of the many documents that are evidence of the fact that the KLA terrorised the Albanian population itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell me the date of the anti-terrorist operation at Jezerce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember the exact date, but it was towards the end of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, until when did you stay in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us as briefly as possible what the security situation was in Kosovo and Metohija when KFOR and UNMIK arrived.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: KFOR entered while I was still there, the 12th of June, and then a hunt against the Serbs and the Roma and all other non-Albanians started. They were killed in streets, thrown out of their homes. Quite literally expelled from their homes. According to the official statistics, over 40.000 Serb houses were torched, razed to the ground. Fifteen thousand houses and apartments were taken by Albanians while their rightful owners are suffering in refugee centres in Serbia and elsewhere. Over 3.000 non-Albanians were kidnapped and killed. Those who were killed are still missing persons. Even their graves cannot be found. Only in the territory of Urosevac, which at the end of the war had about 2.510 houses, 3.210 [as interpreted] houses were razed to the ground. There were 450 Serb apartments. One apartment was torched, and all the others were usurped like the houses that I referred to a few moments ago, because they were not destroyed as they were good for living.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mentioned -- you mentioned official statistics Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there. Where can we find these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Belgrade, at the official statistics office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean they're not in your binders? No. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not in these binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Over what period are you saying these events occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The period from the 12th of June, 1999, onwards. Practically until the present day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're talking about a long period of time. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such things are going on even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This destruction of houses and killing and kidnapping, how much of this happened immediately after the protection force of the UN came, so under their auspices?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ninety-nine per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What is the document contained in tab 91?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document contained in tab 91 is one of the largest Orthodox cemeteries where unidentified Serbs were buried in Kosovo and Metohija. It is in Dulje. Dulje is an elevation between Suva Reka and Stimlje. On this locality, the members of the multinational force buried unidentified Serbs who were found by the road, in ditches, in houses, and other places. The members of the multinational forces found them. In addition to this cemetery, in the area of Pristina at Dragovdan there is another such cemetery with unidentified persons, mostly of Serb ethnicity, and about 400 persons were buried there, about 400 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you said Orthodox cemetery, you meant to say that this is the place where 820 Serbs were buried?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not really a cemetery.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a proper cemetery, a graveyard with any religious markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have these photographs in colour, or can we only see these black and white ones?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, since you're a career policeman and you were chief of the Urosevac SUP for many years, and since I assume that you still follow events in Kosovo and Metohija, could you compare the crime rates before and after the arrival of KFOR?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to respond, but let me just try to find something, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what's the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance is that this fully refutes the accusations levelled here or, rather, written by who knows who, namely that during the rule of Serbia in Kosovo the population was mistreated, killed, et cetera. More people lost their lives after the arrival of the protection force than in several decades before that, in all forms of violence in Kosovo and Metohija, and this all pertains to the time when there is not a single soldier or policeman from Serbia there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Court's looking for me. It seems wholly irrelevant to me, but I know the Court's generous in its approach to the Defence evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm not allowing that question. And if you don't have any more questions, you should just stop and let us move on, get on with the case. Generally, you utilise the last part of your examination to make certain points which are not forensic. If you are finished, then you're finished, and let us begin the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, among other things, this shows that if this were really a Court, and if this were really a Prosecution, somebody else should be on trial here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've cut you off. So conclude your examination-in-chief if you have no further questions to put.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, thank you for testifying. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We skipped tab 66. We have to consider what to do with that tab. And I remember we haven't dealt with tab 76 and 78. In tab 76, Mr. Milosevic, the accused, showed us two video clips which he said he didn't intend to show us, and so we'll not admit 76, but I'm minded to admit 77 and 78. And 77 is not translated, so we'll mark it for identification. The remaining matter would be tab 66. Upon Chamber's recommendation, we skipped over those tabs and we went directly to the Racak event, and I recommended the accused to come back to those tabs if necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for 78, I thought it was admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. 78.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the rest until the end, until the end of the last binder. Thank you. And as for 65 and 66, I am grateful to Mr. Kwon for reminding me. There is a number of exhibits inside that have been partially admitted, and you will find the references attached. The purpose of tendering these is to have admitted the documents that haven't been admitted yet and originate from the Urosevac SUP that was headed by Colonel Janicevic at the relevant time. It is on these documents that certain assessments, conclusions and initiatives were based that led to specific measures and actions to combat terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, any observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 65 and 66, aren't these the ones that appear --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are these the ones that are largely duplicative of material we've received elsewhere? I've made my objections about the generality of producing material -- producing that material through other witnesses, but given the position we're in, I would have thought it probably sensible to have, as it were, the full set and you can make what you can of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wish to check one more thing, because we skipped over certain documents since you insisted, or Mr. Kwon insisted. I want to make sure that tab 67, which is a request of the Malopoljce company of that brigade, the KLA, and the following analysis of security related events that preceded the action in Racak were admitted, tabs 67 and 68. I can't see from my notes whether these have been admitted or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let me just deal with 66. Ms. Higgins had produced a tabulation, 17 documents which have not yet been admitted in evidence. We'll admit those documents. However, those that are not translated are marked for identification pending translation. This same ruling is given in relation to tab 65, that is to say the eight documents identified by Ms. Higgins will be admitted, but those that are not translated will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I don't think Mr. Milosevic dealt with 67 and 68. Correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: That is correct, according to my records where 67, 68, and I think also 69 were not dealt with by Mr. Milosevic. There is one point arising, Your Honours, which is, from my records, tab 51 had not been ruled upon. Again, I stand to be corrected. You may recall that this was a document, again a Ministry of the Interior document which was a Jasovic document, and concern was raised by His Honour Judge Bonomy about the date, which was the 28th of May, 2004, that it in fact relates to events in Kacanik on the 5th of April, 1999. It falls again within the category of the criminal reports that have been admitted to date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: My record is it was not dealt with. I have the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it was dealt with. Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it was admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have dealt with the admission of all the documents produced in examination-in-chief. What's the point about 67 and 68?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 68 is an already exhibited document in D299, so there is no use to be limited again. And the only remaining is tab 67, if you'd like to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I skipped those documents because you insisted that I move on to specific matters, but I had originally intended to ask the witness about the contents of these documents and to give us a brief comment as to whether it fitted with their information about KLA activity from the relevant time. This is a document from the 28th of December, 1998, only 20 days or so before the anti-terrorist operation in Racak, and it refers precisely to the activity of the 161st Brigade that was active in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, put very briefly, then, the questions you wanted to put on 67 -- 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have this document, 67?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is the first document in binder 4, if you have the same format.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is this document about?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a request to the 161st Brigade, the Malopoljce company, to rally some workers and to have them report to the commander of the company to perform certain works.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this relevant to the Racak area?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Malopoljce, Racak, and Rance are all in the same brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Malopoljce, Racak, and Rance are all one whole?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The digging of trenches, communicating trenches and bunkers, can that be qualified as a military or a civilian activity on the part of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that trenches, communicating trenches, and bunkers were dug in Malopoljce, Racak, Petrovo village, and Rance, and did you take that into account when deciding to carry out an anti-terrorist operation?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document testifying to the military activities of the KLA in the area of Racak in tab 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, where was this document recovered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also in Jezerce after the anti-terrorist operation. In April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll mark it for identification pending translation. Before we adjourn, I wanted to clarify, Mr. Milosevic, that the -- whenever I make remarks about the manner in which you present your case, I am not to be understood as suggesting that there is any burden on you to do anything. The burden remains at all times on the Prosecution. And it's a very relevant and important legal issue. For example, in relation to the question of deportation and flights from particular villages, if there is evidence that NATO bombed Village A and there is an allegation in the indictment that people fled from Village A because of Serb crimes committed on them, then in my view the specific evidence which has been led of NATO bombing on Village A could very well give rise to the inference that the flights were due to the bombing. And if that inference is of the same weight as the inference that the flights were due to Serb violence, then the burden of proof being on the Prosecution would, in my view, mean that that burden has not been discharged because the inferences are of equal weight. So it's a very important legal issue. And if you would concentrate specifically in relation to NATO bombing, I think, on showing where the bombing was, then I think your case -- your case would be strengthened. So don't just rely on mass bombing but show that there was a bombing in relation to a specific village in relation to which there is an allegation of deportation due to Serb violence, and then a question may be raised as to whether the Prosecution has discharged its onus in relation to that particular allegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 12:45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, you've been a policeman for many years. Do you regard yourself as essentially a professional policeman?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Being a policeman is your principal or was your principal function in life?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, principal function in life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have any other major functions?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd tell us what they were.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the president of the municipality in Strpce from the 15th of July, 1992, in fact, until the 15th of July, 1995. And I was a popular deputy in the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were a member of the Serbian parliament. And just remind us, please, which party you were a member of.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the accused's party. And what years were you a member of parliament for his interest in the parliament?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I represented the interests of the people who elected me, that's all. My electoral basis was Kosovo and Metohija of the Urosevac, Kacanik, Strpce, and Stimlje municipalities. I was a deputy from 1993, January, to about the year 2000, I think October 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So although you hadn't told us about this, you were actually a politician for the totality of the period of the Kosovo crisis, yes?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, is to be a member of parliament not to be a politician? It's different in your country?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that doesn't mean that you're a politician. That doesn't mean that you're a politician, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You went to the parliament and you took part in the votes. Do they have discussions in your parliament?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they have votes in your parliament?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there's voting, just like in any parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you're elected by some people to represent their interests at a parliament where discussions are held and votes taken. Doesn't that make you a politician?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially, yes, but not wholly. Not in any substantial way, because professionally I was a policeman. Professionally, I was a policeman. I was president of the Assembly while I held that function, but everything else was volunteer work. I worked in the interests of the citizens who had elected me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that anything bad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You were a member of parliament while you were also a policeman. I just want to know as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just at one period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the four years from 1995, is it, until 1999, when you left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course during your seven years as a deputy for the party of which this accused was the leader, you got to know him personally, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him just once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was it by any chance -- was it just oversight that you didn't tell us about this part of your history when you told us about your background?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true that I didn't state it. I said that I was a popular deputy, a national deputy. I apologise. Perhaps you didn't hear when I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps we didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I certainly have no recollection of picking that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, as a professional policeman, and as you explained you were, did you go on training courses anywhere around the world to look at other police forces?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed secondary school for internal affairs in Sremska Kamenica and that school dealt with the training and equipping a policeman. I graduated in 1971, began working on the 1st of July, 1971 in the provisional secretariat in Pristina at that time, and I worked -- I was in Pristina until the 1st of January, 1972. From the 1st of January, 1972, until the 15th or, rather, the 1st of July, 1992, I did various jobs in the Secretariat of the Interior in Urosevac. I was a policeman, a deputy commander, a chief of police station, an inspector for crime prevention, an inspector for general crime, head of the department for general crime, and so on. Deputy commander of the 6th Battalion of special police units at that time that were under establishment. I was a policeman in the Strpce municipality, leader of the sector, so I went through all the different police jobs and assignments. I have answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... courses anywhere around the world to look at any other police forces?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not around the world, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody went. None of us went around the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm only interested in this period really, 1995 to 1999, and I just want a very general answer at the moment. Do you think the police station at Urosevac, where you were in charge, met the highest standards of police service in the Western world, or do you think it fell short in any way?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I can tell you is this: Depending from which angle of vision you look at it, in some areas we were head of the countries of Western Europe. In other respects, we lagged behind, depending on what you're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about lagging behind. You know what we're concerned with, and we'll come to it later in my questioning of you if there's time, but in terms of lagging behind, did lagging behind involve the using violence on people when they were in police custody? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was never resorted to, at least not while I was head of SUP and an inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Janicevic, as the boss between 1995 and 1999, any allegations of violence, any practices of violence, any public condemnation of the police station for violence would, of course, be something that would concern you greatly, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If in the period 1995 to 1999 there was any allegations that violence was practised at your police station, if there was any public - that's written - condemnation of your police station for being a place where violence occurred, that would concern you, as the boss, very much, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course it would be of concern and certain measures would be taken. Quite certainly we did that. And in individual cases there were abuses and overstepping authority by policemen and persons in authority, and then legal measures were resorted to. Many were let go or dismissed as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you now saying that there were practices in your police station that were unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said during the examination-in-chief, that there were such instances and that measures were taken to prosecute the people behaving in unlawful ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Anybody ever prosecuted for beating up a prisoner or torturing a prisoner or electrocuting a prisoner or anything like that? Not a prisoner, a person detained.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you got that from. I don't have that information that somebody in my police station beat somebody using electrocuting methods or things like that. It's just not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Finally on this topic at this stage: It's a big police station, we've seen a picture of it, but do you think that you had a good working knowledge of what was going on in your police station, or do you think there was a possibility that there were rogue elements in your police station that could do things without your knowing what they were up to?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did have knowledge. Had anything happened untoward in the police station, I would have been informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's turn now, then, please, to your exhibit tab 70. I've got --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that, Mr. Nice. Mr. Janicevic, how much of your time was taken up by being a member of parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not much. Two or three days a month at the maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were you paid for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My place of work was the Ministry of the Interior, and that's what I received a salary for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did that apply to all members of the Serb Assembly, that they didn't receive any payment for that service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There were certain deputies who worked permanently in the Assembly, and they received salaries and had all rights pertaining to their job there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. So how did the deputies live? I mean, did they have other jobs, like you did, if they were not paid a salary for being a member of parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A part of the members of parliament that didn't have a permanent job elsewhere in another institution or company did receive salaries in parliament, and then they were permanent working members there. Those who had permanent jobs outside parliament or the Assembly had their professional vocation, and they received salaries where they were permanently employed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So if you didn't have a job elsewhere, then you would receive a salary as a member of parliament.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at -- can we just look at these maps, tab 70, please. Now, Your Honours will recall that I was the fortunate recipient of colour versions last week. It looks as though the Chamber may have got colour versions itself, or has it not? Has the Chamber got colour versions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have those, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On what date, Mr. Janicevic, were these maps prepared?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These maps were prepared the day before I left for The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Uh-huh. What date was that?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In preparation for this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What date was that?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a Sunday, or perhaps Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two weeks ago, one week ago, three weeks ago? Give us a clue.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Three weeks ago on a Sunday or the previous Saturday or Friday these maps were prepared. Who drew them?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said last time: The commander of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What you actually said was that they were prepared -- at least, this is what you said in English, you said that the maps were prepared in cooperation with Milan Lecic, but I actually want you to be a little more precise for us if you'd be so good. Shall we go back right to the beginning of these maps. Whose idea was it to prepare the maps?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean whose idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I thought it was quite a simple question, Mr. Janicevic, but if you'd like, I'll break it down. Which person decided to prepare the maps?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In preparation for this trial, I talked to the company commander and the subject was anti-terrorist action in Racak, and I asked him to make me a dynamic overview or schematic of the whole operation from start to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he prepared these maps in response to that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the answer to my very simple question whose idea was it, it was your idea.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, you're not a lawyer, are you?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And have you been following the case in detail or have you been allowing it to have its long life on its own and not been bothering to follow it? What of that, which?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So -- but not very much?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As much as was needed, not too much. As much as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you said to Lecic -- well, let's again take our time, shall we? Who put you together with Lecic? Or let me ask the question in another simpler way: Whose idea was it that you should meet Lecic?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My idea to meet Lecic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So your idea to meet Lecic. Your idea to produce a dynamic map. And what gave you the -- what made you think it would be a good idea to have a dynamic map?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a simple reason: To remind me of the events that took place more than six years ago, a full six years ago. And six years is quite a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To remind you, why, because you couldn't remember, and you needed someone to help you? Is that what you mean by "to remind me"?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that's not it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, pause again.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you could remember, you could have drawn your own map, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't because I'm not a professional in map drawing. That's one point. And secondly, I wasn't in all the segments of anti-terrorist operations. I wasn't included in all the segments, and so I wasn't -- I didn't remember all of these events. And during the examination-in-chief, I said that I did all this on the basis of the reports that would come in to me from the terrain, from the field, from responsible people in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if we look at the first map, 0300 to 0830, have you got that one in front of you? We can't actually tell which bits of these blue, pale blue, and red lines are your memory and which bits are Lecic's memory, can we? We just don't know.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both parts are both mine and Lecic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's lost on me and of course I don't have the code to help me. But let's just look at a little bit of this, shall we? Let's look at -- do you see the left hand, the middle of the page towards the left, with the pale blue and the dark blue curves that look as though they're sort of eyebrows, really, there are four of them. Do you see those four, pale blue and dark blue, pointing towards the right roughly? Do you see those four?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before Lecic spoke to you, would you have been able to draw the top one of those four?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this circle around Racak or the four curves at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll hold it up and you can see what I'm pointing to if your length of vision is satisfactory. Do you see that one there, that little one? I'm making it easy. I just want to go for a little point and see are you -- Somebody's drawn and you've produced a blue, two blue lines pointing to the right, and I just wanted to know if this is your memory, if you could have done this all on your own, or if this is Lecic's memory. Help us, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of both my memory and Lecic's memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So this is a joint one, is it, two lines and both of you could do it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you I didn't do the lines. Lecic did the lines, but on the basis of memory, where the lines should be placed and where they should have been. They represent trenches in which the terrorists were located until 0630 hours. They're not ordinary lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Give us a picture of the preparation. You see, this map is going to be very important for the Court and we need to know all we can about it. Give us a picture the two of you the day before you came here. Are you sitting at a desk with Lecic, just of two of you, and he's saying, I think the line was here, and you're saying sort of there but slightly more to the right, or did you draw a line and he agreed? Just sort of give us a picture of how this map came to be drawn, Mr. Janicevic. So perhaps was somebody else there. There may have been a professional map drawer, or a legal associate, or a clerk.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Just a moment. I said and I claim again, I don't know how to draw maps. Milan Lecic drew the map and I was with him. On the basis of the chronological sequence of events, the time line in Racak, that's how we drew up the map, and based on our recollections of the events or, rather, the recollection of the event that took place on the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Uh-huh. All right. Well, can you give us -- I don't -- my last question on this little detail: Can you give us the picture? Can you describe to us if it's Lecic sitting there drawing it or if it's a clerk drawing it and you describing what happened, saying, oh, yes, there were some trenches there? What is it? Just help us.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lecic said, since I didn't have occasion to see the trenches over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He said this is where they were, and you said, "All right." Is that it?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Now, before we -- I want you to stay with this map because there's something I want to ask you about it and the other maps in just a second, but you told us about a fire at Pristina police station, I think, where some documents disappeared. Was any one of those documents a document of materiality, of significance, so far as Racak is concerned, that had been prepared by you?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean did a document have material importance for Racak which I prepared? Is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Uh-huh, and went up in the flames.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this, you see: All the documents linked to the anti-terrorism in Racak and the anti-terrorist operation in Racak were sent on to the MUP staff or, rather, was sent on by the MUP staff because a request was made from the commission to establish what had actually happened in Racak, and one example of that set of documents was also sent to the public prosecutor, to the district public prosecutor. Now, I can't remember all the documents in that set of documents. However, it was certainly relevant documentation which pertained to what actually happened that day, from the minutes of the on-site investigation, the photographic material, the Official Notes and reports, the various other reports, and everything else necessary to substantiate evidence for the anti-terrorist action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's break that answer down into a few little bits. You kept no copy of the documents you sent on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you not want an answer to -- I thought the question was whether any documents that this witness personally had prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the question and I'm grateful. Your Honour is quite right, I should have pressed for it now. I probably was going to come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You heard Judge Bonomy's reminder. Could you answer the question: Was a document of significance for Racak that you prepared one of those that went up in flames?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just part of the documents were created with this time line of the events in Racak. I prepared that personally. The rest were prepared by the employees of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have a separate question, unless you're pursuing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying also, Mr. Janicevic, that a copy of all the documents that you had relating to Racak was also sent to the public prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And could now be obtained from there if -- instead of any that may have been destroyed in the police office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do believe that they could be obtained, but it is in the office of the public prosecutor in Pristina, district public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have any efforts been made to obtain them, these missing documents?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you. You're the witness.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were not able to invest efforts of that kind because we didn't have the contacts with the people who were in the public prosecutor's office today. I talked to the district public prosecutor on one occasion, however, before I came here, a month or a month and a half before, and asked him whether there were any documents linked to Racak and all the events that took place in the area, and he said -- he told me that everything had remained in the archives of the prosecutor's office in Pristina and that he could not pull any of those documents out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So no doubt you told this piece of information to accused's legal associates and they could have been in a position to have approached the Pristina office, couldn't they? It's very easy.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legal associates?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's break this question and answer down. What's the name of the person you spoke to in the office of the prosecutor in Pristina? You see, then we can speak to him ourselves. What's his name?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Slavko Stevanovic, district public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the second thing is: The legal associates of this accused who were helping you prepare to give evidence could have picked up the telephone, written a letter, sent an e-mail to Mr. Stevanovic to try and get these documents, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, Mr. Stevanovic is a refugee, a displaced person just like me, and he is in Krusevac. He doesn't have access to the public prosecutor's office in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. In which case the associates could have picked up the telephone and contacted the people who now hold the archive in Pristina and asked for the documents, but they didn't. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No? Why couldn't they have done that?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know why they couldn't have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at this first map in a little bit more detail, but before we do, back to the drawing board, as it were, back to that Saturday or Friday or whenever it was when this map's being drawn. Who is there in the office? There's you, there's Milan Lecic. Who else?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one else.
